en.title: Lanterns Officially Ditches Green Lantern's Most Ridiculous Weakness
en.summary: The HBO series 'Lanterns' has taken a significant step away from classic Green Lantern lore. In its latest episode, the showrunners have seemingly retired a long-standing, often criticized, vulnerability of the power rings.
en.body:
Fans of cosmic weirdness and, more importantly, fans of *not* having their favorite heroes constantly hampered by a color, have reason to celebrate. The penultimate episode of HBO's **Lanterns** has finally, and officially, waved goodbye to one of the Green Lanterns' most infamous and frankly, ridiculous, weaknesses: their inability to affect anything yellow.

For decades, the power rings wielded by heroes like Hal Jordan and John Stewart faltered in the presence of the color yellow. This peculiar vulnerability, first introduced in the Silver Age of comics, meant that a strategically placed yellow object could render a Lantern utterly powerless. Imagine a superhero whose primary tool is imagination and willpower, defeated by a banana or a school bus. While some storylines attempted to explain or even overcome this limitation, it remained a persistent, often eye-rolling, aspect of the mythology. However, **Lanterns** season 1 episode 7 saw **Hal Jordan** and **John Stewart** venturing off-world, finding themselves in a decidedly yellow environment. Crucially, Hal's ring continued to function, powering his holographic companion and presumably, himself, without issue. This move signals a bold departure, one that prioritizes the characters and their capabilities over a relic of comic book history that has long outlived its narrative utility.

## A Bold Departure from the Source

The decision to discard the yellow weakness is more than just a minor tweak; it's a fundamental rethinking of what a Green Lantern can and should be in a modern adaptation. Showrunners **Marc Guggenheim** and **Seth Grahame-Smith**, who have navigated the complex task of bringing these iconic characters to HBO, have opted to streamline the lore for maximum dramatic impact. This allows for more dynamic action sequences and a stronger focus on the intergalactic law enforcement aspect of the Green Lantern Corps, rather than constantly finding contrived ways to circumvent a built-in limitation. It’s a move that respects the spirit of the characters – their power, their bravery, their ability to overcome any obstacle – by removing an obstacle that felt increasingly arbitrary and less about genuine stakes and more about a quirky, outdated rule.

## What This Means for Fans

For the dedicated fanbase of **Lanterns**, this is a significant development that underscores the show's commitment to crafting a compelling, contemporary take on the Green Lantern saga. The series, starring **Kyle Chandler** as Hal Jordan and **Aaron Pierre** as John Stewart, has already delved into a dark, Earth-based mystery, and this narrative choice suggests a willingness to adapt and evolve the source material where necessary. It frees up the writers to explore more complex threats and character interactions without the constant need to justify why a Lantern is struggling against a yellow brick. This move prioritizes narrative coherence and character empowerment, ensuring that the focus remains on the compelling stories being told, not on an arbitrary limitation that has long been a point of contention among fans. It’s a clear signal that **Lanterns** is here to forge its own path, one that honors the legacy while boldly stepping into the future.

## What's Next

The season finale of **Lanterns** is fast approaching, and with this major lore change cemented, the stakes are higher than ever as Hal and John face the unknown consequences of their actions. Details for a potential second season have not yet been announced.

content_raw: This article contains spoilers for Lanterns season 1 episode 7 . Fans of cosmic weirdness in Green Lantern stories, rejoice. The penultimate episode of Lanterns finally gets out of Nebraska, and gets off of Earth altogether to go… somewhere. We don’t yet know where John Stewart and the Hal-o-Gram went (my money’s on Qward, within the Anti-Matter Universe), but we do know one thing about it: it’s really, really yellow. And, yet, Hal’s ring keeps the Hal-o-Gram running. That observation means nothing to those only know Green Lantern mythos through Lanterns. Of course the Hal-o-Gram would still be around because we want as much Kyle Chandler as we can get. But to comic book readers, especially those who love the Silver and Bronze Age comics that inform so much of the show, the Hal-o-Gram’s persistence stands out. That’s because, for most of Green Lantern history, the Lanterns ‘ power rings would not work on anything yellow. Shortly after first getting his power ring from Abin Sur in 1959’s Showcase Comics #22, by John Broome and Gil Kane, Hal Jordan stops a missile from destroying Coast City and then traces the signal back to the bad guys’ hideout. The ring allows Hal to phase through the hideout wall, and he deflects their bullets with ease. But when one of the hoods throws a lamp at him, Hal gets bonked on the head and crumples to the floor, allowing them to escape. Why? Because the lamp was yellow. Up until relatively recently, Green Lantern power rings would not work on anything yellow. The weakness was a revision of the original Green Lantern concept, the one introduced in 1940’s All-American Comics #16, by Bill Finger and Martin Nodell. Even though the first Green Lantern Alan Scott was not part of the Green Lantern Corps and had abilities based in magic instead of (very comic-booky) science, his ring had a weakness. It would not work on anything made of wood, leading to similarly embarrassing moments when he gets knocked out by a gangster with a lamp. Of course, both the weaknesses to wood and yellow were initially little more than genre conventions, an excuse to create tension in a story (fun fact: the wood weakness actually predates the introduction of Kryptonite, which isn’t mentioned until a 1943 episode of the radio show, The Adventures of Superman ). But over the years, writers began to give more reasons for the weakness. First, it was just that yellow was the later, it was a necessary impurity, some aspect of the power harnessed by the Guardians that could not be avoided. However, the most significant explanation came from writer Geoff Johns in the 2002 series Green Lantern: Rebirth . Set after Hal Jordan had become the villainous Parallax, and after he heroically sacrificed himself to reignite the sun, and after he sought redemption as the ghostly superhero the Spectre, Rebirth had to both revive Jordan and to let him off the hook for everything he did as Parallax
